When you compare the number of people who vote to the number of seats up for election, the percentage of the voters who actually make a difference in a given election is so small it’s not even worth measuring.  Even if you’re the 10th most likely voter to sway the election, you still have a one in 10,000 chance of making any difference at all. We also have a fairly compelling theory for why we have this phenomena.  To make any meaningful difference to the election outcome, you have to be in a state or locality where the candidates are close enough in votes that your vote could be a significant percentage of the difference between them.

prompt: How are locks picked?

Picking is when you try to physically manipulate a lock to get the bolt to move, which requires the skill of feeling for the right places to pick and pressing in just the right ways, and can be time consuming and somewhat unreliable.  Bumping involves using a tool or your knuckles to apply pressure in the lock to move the bolt a little bit.  Drilling is when you cut a small hole in the door and the lock and get into the lock that way.  Manipulation involves using a tool to move the bolt directly without picking or bumping, using either a tool that works in combination with the lock, or by physically manipulating the lock with your hands.  Do you want me to tell you more about this?

A relatively common type of lock is a pin tumbler lock, which consists of a number of pins set in a cylinder, and requires the lock to be “picked” to align the pins with holes in the barrel of the lock.  There are different styles of “picking” locks, but the general principle is to tap or pry the pins (or “tumblers”) into place so that they can fit through the corresponding hole.

Most of her work seems to portray the people of Germany in a sort of wistful way, or it can be an affirmation of the human condition.  One of the more striking things is the way she focuses on the people around her, rather than herself.  Her main focus is on the art of capturing the human presence, not the woman behind the camera.

The latter film includes an interview with Goering, and perhaps the most memorable scene of the entire film, where Hitler steps onto the balcony at the party, and the crowd goes wild.
